entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Flavius Strategius Apion, a patrician and jurist of the Eastern Roman Empire, achieved the singular distinction of being the sole Roman consul for the year 539 CE, a rare occurrence in the late antique period that underscored the consolidation of imperial authority under Emperor Justinian I. Born into the immensely wealthy and politically influential Apion family of Oxyrhynchus, Egypt, Strategius Apion inherited a legacy of administrative service and vast landholdings, positioning him at the apex of the Byzantine aristocracy. His career spanned a critical juncture in the empire's history, marked by Justinian's ambitious legal reforms and attempts to reconquer the Western Roman Empire, during which Apion served as a crucial administrative and legal pillar.

Strategius Apion's career was characterized by significant administrative and legal responsibilities. Prior to his consulship, he held the esteemed title of *comes sacrarum largitionum* (Count of the Sacred Largesses) between 537 and 539 CE, overseeing the imperial treasury and tax collection. His unique sole consulship in 539 CE, a position traditionally shared by two individuals, symbolized the dwindling practical significance of the office while simultaneously affirming the emperor's supreme power to appoint even its most prestigious incumbents. As a jurist, Apion was deeply embedded in the legal traditions of the Eastern Roman Empire, undoubtedly contributing to the intellectual environment that facilitated the monumental codification efforts of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*.
